utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. THE COURT: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Mark Harmon, Lorna Bolton, Carmela Javier appearing for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all the participants in this proceedings. Today we have Milos Androvic, Tina Drolec, Daniela Tasic, Gregor Guy-Smith, and Novak Lukic for Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We would call General Dorde Curcin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Morning, sir. Could you state your name and spell your last name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: My name is Curcin, Dorde. I'm not sure how to spell it. That's C-u-r-c-i-n.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prior to coming to court today, did you provide a statement under oath on the 1st of August 2006 before an investigative judge of the 2nd Municipal Court in Belgrade as part of criminal proceedings against an accused Blagoje Govedarica?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement against Blagoje Govedarica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the 6th of November, 2007, pursuant to a request for assistance by the office of the Prosecutor, were you summoned to the Belgrade district court war crimes Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On that date did you provide a statement before Judge Dragan Plasnic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I gave that statement before the Judge Dragan Plasnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before you gave that statement, were you warned of the consequences of giving false testimony?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you gave your statement to Judge Plasnic, was I present along with a investigator Mr. Bretton Randal and Mr. Novak Lukic who is Defence counsel for General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, and an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the 24th of August, 2007, did you voluntarily provide to the Defence in the Odonic case a statement?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I apologise, could you tell me what year you mean?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the 5th of October, 2007, did you testify as a Defence witness in this institution on behalf of General Odonic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you require a subpoena to attend those proceedings, or did you attend voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Which proceedings do you mean, the -- this proceedings or the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm referring to the proceedings that occurred with General Odonic where you were a witness and you testified in those proceedings on the 5th of October, 2007. My question is, did you require a subpoena to appear in those proceedings, or did you appear voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I came voluntarily at the request of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of these proceedings, General Curcin, were you contacted by an OTP investigator on the 6th of February, 2009, and asked to attend these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: On that day someone tried to get in touch with me, but I refused to speak with him until the procedure as envisaged by our laws was followed, because at the time I did not have a waiver on official secrets, nor had I received a subpoena or a summons from my court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you require a subpoena in order to attend these proceedings today?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Had the procedure been followed, I would have come gladly voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you receive a subpoena to attend these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you were contacted yesterday by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor in order to review your statements and a proofing session, did you refuse to do so?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prior to these proceedings, General Curcin, have you talked to anybody about your testimony in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell us, General Curcin, about your military background. Take us through your career, please.

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I completed the military academy land forces in 1967, and I became a lieutenant. I went through many levels from commander of a platoon and company battalion Brigade. I also performed various duties as an instructor in military schools. I had operative duties in the Brigade corps and army. And I finished my career as Lieutenant-General, the chief of the first administration in the General Staff of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Amongst the posts that you held, General Curcin, were you the chief of operations and training in the 1st Army?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, for five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what were those years?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: From 1983 -- I apologise, from 1993 up until 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When were you appointed to the rank of major-general?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: In 1995 on the 16th of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether the witness said June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, was it in June, or was it in July of 1995? The interpreter didn't understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: On the 16th of June, on army day, that was the army day of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were you ever assigned to the Yugoslav Army General Staff, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, the decision to transfer me to a duty in the General Staff was issued to me prior to new year 1998, and on the 13th of January, 1999, I became the chief of the first administration of the General Staff. And I was -- I remained in this duty up until the 30th of September in the year of 2000. I apologise, I think it was 2000. Or rather, 2001. I'm not absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when did you retire from the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: On the 30th of September. I think 2001, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long have you known Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: For over 30 years now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you first become acquainted with Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I was first acquainted to his -- to Ratko Mladic when we attended the command staff academy together about 32 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever have any assignments with Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes. We were battalion commanders in the same Brigade, in the 3rd Army in Macedonia. We did many -- we had many assignments together as captains 1st class.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How would you characterise your relationship with Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this topic is irrelevant, the facts that we are discussing now, so I would ask my colleague, Mr. Harmon, to explain what the relevance of these questions is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, then I would ask the witness to be excused so the explanation isn't made in his presence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, General, would you please excuse us. You can stand down for a short while, we'll call you back in another couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The relevance of this question, Your Honour, is that it is our position that this witness had a very close personal relationship with the the witness. I'm going to be asking him questions about General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, you said this witness has a very close relationship with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I didn't mean to say that, with General Mladic. It is our position, Your Honour, that this witness, that experience may colour the testimony of this witness when I ask him other questions, and I think it's important that the Court understand the relationship and when listening to the answers of this witness because there will be some questions that will probe about events that he had a hand in, in our view -- that he had a hand in, in secreting General Mladic from the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In doing what to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He was involved in harbouring General Mladic from the public. That is our position. And I think the Court would be informed to know about his relationship with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness, as far as I can see from the summary of his testimony, I believe that in context of the facts that are mentioned there, that is what the Prosecutor should focus on, and there is no mention on his close relationship with General Mladic. And that's why I felt it was irrelevant to the case at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if the witness could be called back into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we can call the witness back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Curcin, how would you characterise your relationship with Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: General Mladic and I are good friends. We also attended school together, and we are also personal or family friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General Curcin, what is your relationship with General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: General Perisic is also someone I went through training together. We attended the national defence school together. He was the Chief of General Staff when I was there, and I can say that he was a mate, a pal. Just a pal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you inform us of -- actually, what was the relationship between General Mladic and General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I am afraid I cannot describe that because I don't actually know what the relationship was, except that I know that all three of us were in the same group in the national defence school together, and we -- we've known each other since then as colleagues. As for any more details, I'm not sure I could help with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you asked by Judge Plazinic to describe the relationship between General Perisic and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes, but I did not really want to discuss that because anything I would say about it would be speculation because I am unable to testify to those facts firsthand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the term in your language "kum"?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what does -- can you define that term for the Trial Chamber. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: When two people get married, they have to have witnesses, two witnesses, and those people are called kum. So a kum is not quite a relative, but it is a very valuable, dear friend and it goes on through the family for a long time. This kum is also supposed to name the children once they are born, to give them their first names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a relationship of kum between General Perisic and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, that's not true. That's just an invented story.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were General Mladic and General Perisic related by marriage in any way, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar, General Curcin, with the facilities, the Yugoslav Army facilities at Rajac and Stragari?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, in Stragari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe -- let's start with the facilities at Rajac, can you describe the facilities at Rajac, please.

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a hotel at Rajac?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: There is something that we call a hotel at Rajac, but it's not really a hotel by any standards. It is a small area enclosed or fenced in by a stone fence, and there is wire on three sides. These facilities are meant or rest and recreation. There is a football pitch, a volleyball and basketball pitch and also a very nice park where you can take walks and rest. There is also a sort of lobby at the very entrance and then three small homes, weekend homes, as it were. So this is a facility of -- that perhaps I could describe in further detail if you'd like me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand your statement. This is a facility where VJ soldiers can go and take recreation and take lodging, take rest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, not military, not soldiers, but officers and members of their family, as well as civilians. And this is for a very limited number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say it's for a limited number of people, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, that would mean that about 30 people at most can lodge there at a time, as far as I can recall. Most of these rooms were two bedrooms and that was on the first floor and then on the higher floors, on the second floor there were two bed- and three bedrooms. And on the ground floor, there's a restaurant and a kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there facilities of a similar kind at the facility at Stragari?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. Both these facilities were -- had a different purpose earlier, but then later on when there was no need for that anymore, it was turned Rajac into a recreation and lodging facility. Stragari is a command post used for training. And in certain -- at certain times, officers and commanders would go through training there. There is no hotel there. There is just an administration building, a one-story building; two small houses where the personnel is lodged or accommodated, one room each; and one or two huts where personnel can lodge; several concrete platforms prepared for setting up tents, large tents; parking lots; and a large hall which was built 200 years ago where the command could be stationed so that they can practice certain tactical practices, exercises. So this is a far larger area than the facility at Rajac. Both these facilities are guarded by four to five guards and several guard dogs, and there would be one officer who was in charge of the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Curcin, during the period you were chief of operations and training in the 1st Army, that is from 1993 to 1998, did either or both of those facilities come under your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. I know that I said before the Judge that one of these facility, Rajac, namely, was under my jurisdiction. What I meant then was the division of duties between me and the logistics commander as to who was going to be in charge of this facility so that it could be improved and maintained properly. Generally speaking both these facilities are under the exclusive command of the staff command of the 1st Army, and the staff command is subordinated to the Chief of Staff of the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you said before the Judge of the 2nd municipal court that Rajac specifically came under your jurisdiction, what am I to understand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps it would be a good idea to follow the same practice that we followed so far, to namely put this sentence before the witness so that he can read it, and then he can understand what context the question was put in and what context his answer should be in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting to Mr. Harmon how he should run his case? Or I'm not quite sure what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I apologise if that's how it came across. I just think that the witness should be allowed to see the statement and to read the sentence as he had actually worded it, and I think it would be best to hear what the witness had said actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let's see how Mr. Harmon wants to prosecute the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Curcin, my question to you was when you said before the judge of the 2nd municipal court that Rajac was specifically under your jurisdiction, what am I to understand from that answer?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I would prefer to see the text itself and to read the entire paragraph because I have never seen that statement before, and I can't really remember what I said exactly. So I would like to see what it is that I exactly said there and the entire context, and then I could answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could the statement of General Curcin before the 2nd Municipal Court in Belgrade be put on the monitor. The B/C/S version, please. Could the English as well be placed on the other side of the monitor. If the witness could review his statement, I think we will need to go in the B/C/S version of the statement to the next page, and in the English version we will have to go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, you'll see a part of your previous statement on the monitor. When you get to the bottom, you'll need to keep reading down, and if you will tell us when you've reach the bottom of the page, the Registrar will move the page up for you.

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I probably did not quite understand or correctly understand the question of the Judge. And secondly, it was not I who gave this statement and dictated the text, it was rather a conversation with a judge and then he read out or he wrapped it up for the typist. I have to repeat, the Rajac and Stragari facilities were under the command of the headquarters administration of the 1st Army and the headquarters administration in the chain of command was under the command of the Chief of Staff of the 1st Army. When I said something as it appears here, what I meant was the internal division between me and the logistics assistant who it was to be between the two of us who would take care of the facilities to make them liveable for the people who go to rest there. This had nothing to do with the establishment itself because within per establishment, it is very clear who is responsible for what in the army. Therefore, I apologise if there was a misunderstanding of some sort, but I had no jurisdiction over either one of these two facilities, which means that I didn't have jurisdiction over Rajac either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say, General Curcin, that, and I'm quoting you: "What I meant was the internal division between me and the logistics assistant who it was to be between the two of us who would take care of the facilities to make them liveable for people who would go to rest there," what was the internal division between you and the logistics assistants that you are describing?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: At the very outset the interpreter said internal, "inner," but in fact it was between the two of us, the two of us discussed this issue as to who was to take care to make sure that good conditions existed there so that the officers and their family members can go and spend some time there, rest there, and that is the only way it should be understood and in no other sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So again, when you say "the two of us who took care of good conditions," who were the two people you are talking about, yourself and who else?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Vukovic Ljubisa. But we did not really dwell on this issue, we rather tried through the collegium of the army commanders to ensure what any of the heads requested, and they would need a lot of time to get it through normal channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So let's start first of all, who is Ljubisa Vukovic, who is he, and what is his position in the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Ljubisa Vukovic at the time was a colonel, later he became a general. He was logistics officer. So I was logistic officer for the entire command, and he was the logistic officer, operations officer in the logistics. And for various reasons he took care about this particular facility all this time. One of the reasons that he took care about this facility was that his command used this facility for training from time to time, and my part used Rajac for training of officers and commands for given operations. And this is why we needed optimum conditions when it comes to communications, accommodation, and other prerequisites in order for these two parts of the command to be able to function when they went into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So to be clear, you were the logistics officer for the entire command, do I understand that to be the entire command of the 1st Army?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said that, "I was logistics officer for the entire command." I'm quoting your answer at page 14, lines 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: This was an interpretation error. I never mentioned logistics. I was an operations officer. I was in charge of operations, so I was in charge of operations affairs, rather than logistics. I did not mention logistics in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was then Colonel Vukovic a subordinate of yours?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. Colonel Vukovic was subordinate to the assistant for logistics at the 1st Army Command, and this was Mr. Pantelic. General Pantelic. And General Pantelic was subordinated to the chief of the army. As the operations officer, I was subordinated to -- but truth be said, a year or two later, when General Pantelic left to work at the General staff, Colonel Vukovic became assistant for logistics, so the first person when it comes to logistics in the 1st Army, and he was subordinated to the army commander, we are talking about the 1st Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General, I'm trying to understand part of your answer earlier. You said that along these lines that, the two of us took care that good conditions existed there, meaning at the Rajac facility. What were your responsibilities toward the Rajac facility? What did you do in respect of the Rajac facilities while you were between -- while you were the chief of operations and training in the 1st Army?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Nothing, we simply used this facility from time to time for the purpose of training in order to have as little work as possible in order to find the facility cleaned, prepared, tables positioned as we wanted them, in order to have the communications and heliport prepared and car parking prepared, we insisted to have this through the command of the headquarters administration to have all this prepared before we came there. And this is why I said that we had certain competences, but it would be better to say that we had certain requests as to what needed to be prepared before we came to this facility. We had no other competencies, neither General Vukovic nor myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's my understanding, General Curcin, that the Rajac facility was in a state of either disrepair or it wasn't particularly fit for housing guests during the period from 1995 onwards, and that there was an effort made to rehabilitate the facility in order to make it -- the standards elevated and people could stay there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: To a certain extent, but not entirely. This is the matter before General Vukovic and myself managed to convince the Chief of General Staff and the army commander to make sure that this facility is improved in order to be able to receive guests, until that moment that facility was -- fell out of use because it was not at all used. In order to improve the facility to make sure that certain number of officers and members of their family could go there for vacation, certain things needed to be repaired starting from carpets and curtains and bedding and dishes and all that. So that officers and their families, once they came there, could have their vacation there under proper conditions as prescribed by the command of the Yugoslav Army. So this is what I wanted to say as a way of answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. General Curcin, did you have any decision-making or decision-making in the improvements that were taking place at the Rajac facility?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. And there was no need for that. This issue was discussed at the collegium and the army commander turned this into orders issued to the Chief of General Staff who then issued respective orders. So for example, the asphalt was put on the road, the main gate was repaired, and monument was erected to Misic who fought there in the vicinity during the First World War. Also the external lighting was repaired and different things were done so that when officers came there, either officially or privately, they could find more or less appropriate conditions for their work and vacation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Curcin, did you see General Mladic at the Rajac facility?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you see General Mladic at the Rajac facility?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: In early July of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On how many separate occasions did you see General Mladic at the Rajac facility?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I'm sure I saw him at least once approximately one month later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How did you become aware that General Mladic was at the Rajac facility?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Somebody told me that he was there, and then one weekend I simply went down there to have a walk and some rest, and since he was there we also met each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who told you that General Mladic was at the Rajac facility?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that you went to the Rajac facility on your own and by chance met General Mladic at that facility, or did you go to see General Mladic specifically?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I can't say that for sure, maybe I heard, and that's why I went there. But I used to go to Rajac often, as often as I could. I would go there and spend an entire week with my wife or with my granddaughter, so I went to Rajac quite a lot, but on that specific occasion it could be that I heard from somebody that he was there and I also had some time, and therefore I went there to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How is it possible that General Mladic was at the Rajac facility in July of 1997?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: He was simply there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I can't say that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the Rajac facility a facility for VJ officers?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, it was a facility for officers, members of their family and civilian employees of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what was Ratko Mladic's status?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: As far as I know General Ratko Mladic retired on 1st of March, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Retired from where in March of 2002?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't understand this question, retired from where.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did he retire from in 2002?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I couldn't say this for sure because as far as I know his active military duty ceased following a decree of the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. There may have been another decree prior to this from Republika Srpska whereby he was member of the Army of Republika Srpska, and then this decree was just verified by the decree of the Yugoslav Army. I really don't know these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sir, when you gave testimony under oath to Judge Plazinic on the 6th of November, 2007, were you asked and did you answer -- were you asked about General Mladic's status and did you answer, and I quote: "Ratko Mladic was an active serviceman in the Yugoslav Army until March 2002." Did you provide that answer to Judge Plazinic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Could I see that on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I then have 65 ter -- the identification number 06145678 on the screen. And I'm interested in page 3 of the English. I believe it's page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you possibly enlarge this a bit. Thank you. Yes, I remember this. Could you kindly repeat your question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you tell Judge Plazinic that Ratko Mladic was an active serviceman in the Yugoslav Army until March 2002?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did say this, though there is a procedure which I did not explain on this occasion. First of all --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for just a minute. I'm not asking you about a procedure, I'm asking you whether you gave Judge Plazinic the answer that is in the recorded statement. Now, I want to proceed, General Curcin. I want you to describe your visit with General Mladic at the Rajac facility when you visited him the first time. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: We didn't really do anything. We talked for awhile. It was raining, although it was summer, so we could not walk through the woods. We sat in a hole. We played some chess. We may have played some cards as well. We had lunch together, and in the afternoon I went back to Belgrade. I came to Rajac approximately at 10.30, and I came back to Belgrade during the daylight in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Did you travel to Rajac and make that first visit with your wife?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, who was present with General Mladic on the occasion of your first visit?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: There were several members of his security team. Nobody else that I could recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how were the members of his security team dressed?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I remember that in my statement given before the Judge, I said that they wore the army uniforms, but now I couldn't claim that on the occasion of my very first visit they had uniforms on. At least not all of them. Later on they did, but on that occasion, some of them may have wore uniforms, some of them were in civilian clothes, or maybe all of them were in civilian clothes. Later on all of them, or at least most of them, wore camouflage army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Camouflage army uniforms of what army?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: All the uniforms were similar, but those that I can remember wore the uniforms of our army of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in addition to the persons who were wearing uniforms around General Mladic, did he have his own personal close protection unit?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Apart from the cook and the waiter, there were also several other people who served as his personal guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were in his entourage when you visited General Mladic in Rajac?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: There was nobody around him. These men were hidden away, concealed. They stayed away so they weren't very visible, so I never knew how many of them were present, nor where were they. But I'm sure there were several. More than two or three, but you couldn't really see them or count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said there was a cook. What other types of people were involved or supporting General Mladic at the Rajac facility? You said a cook, what else?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: The waiter, a driver, and that's about it. And in addition to this there were several body-guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How were his body-guards dressed?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to explain awhile ago. Some may have wore uniforms, some wore civilian clothes, that's what I could see. But given that I did not know them personally, they circulated, so I couldn't really tell you how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And who paid for General Mladic's security guards?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: This is what I told you back in Belgrade, I do not know precisely who paid for his security guards. I never came across any payment records, I never saw that any money changed hands. At the time we received salaries on our current accounts as, as we do now, and it was enough for the army IT centre to provide to the Ministry's IT centre certain data, and this is how payment of certain amount was made. In other words, I remember very well what I answered last time, and this is that this security was probably paid by the same source that provided General Mladic's salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was that source?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't know. I assume, as I said the last time, that this was the financial service of the Ministry of Defence. They are the ones who are paying salaries, not the financial service of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct you, General Curcin, to the same statement that is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could go to page 7 of the English. And in the B/C/S I imagine it is the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Curcin, let me ask you this question: You were asked who organised and paid for General Mladic's security guards by Judge Plazinic, and -- or in the proceedings before Judge Plazinic, and you answered: "I do not know who organised and paid for Mladic's security guards. I know that Mladic was in charge of the team, and the men were probably paid by those who paid General Mladic, meaning, the financial service of the Yugoslav Army..." Was that the answer you gave before Judge Plazinic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Please allow me just to find this. Yes, although it seems to me that this was wrongly translated, that he was in charge of the team. I'm not sure. "I do not know who organised and paid for Mladic's security guards, I note that the team was under the chain of command of General Mladic." Yes, this is what I stated, but this is what the Judge dictated to be recorded. The Judge asked a question, he talked to me about this issue, and then he dictated the text to the recorder, so there is nothing I would like to change now. I can just add that the body responsible for payment of salaries is the financial service of the Ministry of Defence. And the financial service of the army simply provides data to the IT sector of the Ministry of Defence who takes care of the payments.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Curcin, the record of interview before Judge Plazinic was prepared, typed, and you had an opportunity to review that interview, did you not? And in fact you had an opportunity to sign the interview after reviewing it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Up to a point. Now, you can recall you were seated on my right, and I did not read this note. I just signed it without reading it. Both your investigator and the interpreter were there in addition to Judge Plazinic and the typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in addition to Mr. Lukic who was counsel for General Perisic, he was also there?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic was there during the first part, and I'm sure that he left at the point where you started putting questions to me, or maybe a little after that. He was -- he had to leave. He did not remain there throughout. And that's not noted in this record. And of course, this record is -- has to do with -- it's an interview relating to a completely different case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First of all, could you indicate whose signature that is at the bottom right-hand side of the B/C/S version that's in front of you on the monitor. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we go to the end of the document in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you see your signature on that page?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can we go to the first page of the B/C/S and the first page of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your evidence, General Curcin, at page 24, line 12 and 13, you said: "This record -- I'm quoting you "this record is, has to do with -- it's an interview relating to a completely different case." Could you go to the top paragraph of this B/C/S version on the right, and you can see that this interview was compiled in connection with cases before the International Criminal Tribunal, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic and the Prosecutor versus Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. You see that?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I can see that, but you know very well and you can remember very well that the first page was not dictated in my presence. It was probably already something that had already been entered into the computer before the interview was started. There was no mention of either Radovan Karadzic or Ratko Mladic, but only of the case against Momcilo Perisic. And you can also see at the end there is no signatures from the Defence counsel here because he was there the first two-thirds of the interview but then he was not there at the very end. So he was probably not there and able to sign it. So in other words, I did know and I was told by Judge Plazinic that this was a case the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic and not the Prosecutor versus Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic. And I again state that this first page was not something that was typed in my presence. There's just a form, it's a template that was already in the computer before I entered the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Curcin, you've described your first visit with General Mladic, and I'd like you to describe -- can you identify when your second visit was with General Mladic at the Rajac facility?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I think it was in late July 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After that visit, was there another visit at Rajac with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: At least another one, but much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was that, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Well, although I really would like to try and recall, I can't, and I can't tell you, but after awhile, he left these facilities, and I can't remember when he returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long was his first visit at the Rajac facility, the one in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it in July 1995? You just said July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: July 1997, I'm sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long was the first visit? How long did General Mladic stay at the Rajac facility?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Again I'm not sure what I am supposed to answer to, whether how long my first visit there was or whether how long he stayed at Rajac in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't make it clear. How long did General Mladic stay at the Rajac facility on his first -- the occasion of his first visit?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: A little over a month perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how long did he stay on the occasion of his second visit?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you visit General Mladic at Rajac between Christmas and Serbian new year in 2002?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, that's an error. I did visit General Mladic between -- sometime between our Serbian new year and the Serbian Christmas which means between the 7th and 14th of January 2002, but this visit was at Stragari, not at Rajac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. When you visited General Mladic at Rajac, did he have other visitors besides yourself?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to. If you can assist me. I'm not certain that I understood your question fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Besides yourself, who else visited General Mladic while he was staying at Rajac?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: On one occasion, General Mladic received a visit from General Perisic who came to be around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this is at the Rajac facility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: This was sometime in the latter part of July, almost in early August 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And at the time General Perisic visited General Mladic at Rajac, what position did he hold in the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: He was the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the visit with General Mladic and General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it vividly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to object, Your Honour. We can leave the date as it is in the transcript on page 27, line --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But because he said, the witness said that General Perisic was the Chief of Staff of the Yugoslav Army, the witness did state so, but I assume that it's an error. So this is on line 14, page 27, I apologise. I mean, the year is totally wrong, let me be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see the error, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The year says 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were asked when did General Perisic visit General Mladic at the Rajac facility, and your answer is recorded as "early August 2007." Is that an error?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely an error. Both of these things, not in early August, but late July, on the eve of the beginning of August in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe the visit that General Perisic and General Mladic had.

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: On a weekend in the morning around 10.30 or 11.00 as they emerged from the facility on the road to take a walk, this was the road between Ljig and Gornje Milanovac, as I was a strolling down the road by the fence where there is a sort of depression, I noticed on the right-hand side next to the fence a vehicle, a dark coloured Audi with dark windows. This is a area where -- this is a no-parking zone, so this is why I noticed this vehicle that was parked there. I went up to the vehicle to see who was there. And then the left, the driver's glass went down, and I noticed that General Perisic was inside. He was dressed in civilian clothes. He was driving the car. There was no security around him. I asked him kindly how he was, and he said, Well, I'm on my way, I went to visit my mother in Kostunici, and I'm on my way to Belgrade. Then I asked him, Why don't you drop by and visit with us? He didn't want to, but then I managed to talk him into it. He turned around his car and drove to the facility. He spent some time there, had conversation with General Mladic. They played some chess, maybe also some table tennis, and a little after dinner, after lunch time, or after they had lunch, he left for Belgrade. So this day I'm not even sure that he actually did have lunch. That was all, his entire visit, and this meeting that I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he say why he didn't want to visit with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention, General Curcin, to the facility at Stragari. Did General Mladic stay a Stragari?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many times did he stay at Stragari following the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: What end of the war? What war?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The end of the war in Bosnia? How many times did General Mladic stay in Stragari?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't really know, and I doubt that he does, because he probably visited there on and off. He would spend there some time and then go back home or some other place, so I can't really tell how long or how often he visited the Stragari facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you visit General Mladic at the Stragari facility following the end of the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Before the war certainly not, but since you are insisting on the period after the war, I suppose I was supposed to understand that to mean after July and August 1997. I did go there and visit a couple of times on my way to inspect some units, or sometimes I would just go to see him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: General, how many times did you visit General Mladic at Stragari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know exactly the number of visits, but more than two to three times. Maybe four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those visits that you paid on General Mladic, were they announced visits? Did you go to see him purposefully? Did you know he was there at Stragari when you stopped at Stragari and visited him?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. As was the case with Rajac, I wasn't always informed or I didn't always know whether -- that he was there or not. I would just stop by and see, and then if he was there, we would have a cup of coffee, and I would be on my way. I never announced my visit so this wasn't the case in Stragari either. We were never in communication in any way either by courier or e-mail or pigeon mail or any other kind of way, so these were just meetings that we had on the go, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So these were chance visits to General Mladic at Stragari, am I to understand your evidence that way?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, both in Stragari and at Rajac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I see. Now, in the time you visited General Mladic at Stragari and at Rajac, were you aware that General Mladic had been indicted by the Tribunal and that there were warrants for his arrest?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I learned of that somewhat later from the media. In other words, I heard of this indictment and also that there was a reward offered and that he was indicted before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question was, during the time that you met with General Mladic at Rajac and Stragari, were you aware that he had been indicted and that there was a warrant issued for his arrest?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I can't recall when it was exactly that I heard of this from the media, but I never had opportunity to see the indictment, so I can't really be more precise in my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you asked this question, the same question, before Judge Plazinic, and did you answer, and I quote: "During the time when I met with Mladic, I heard about the indictment against him." Did you give that answer to Judge Plazinic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: It's quite possible that I answered in that manner, but I'm taking this opportunity now to clarify to you and to the Trial Chamber that it was only later, and I'm not sure exactly what year it was, that I learned that there was an indictment against him. But let me say this, both on that occasion and today, I could have chosen not to answer that question so that I would not be in jeopardy in any way, so that legal action might not be taken against me. But here it is, I did say what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 7 of the English, the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, General Curcin, I'm going to give you an opportunity to review your answer in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I imagine this is on the second to last page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see that part on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps it's on the next page then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, how much longer are you still going to be going?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: With the witness, I will be going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are long past the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought it was 10.30, Your Honour, with the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's quarter past.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, if I finish with this answer, then I'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please zoom in on this particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Second paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I probably did say this in this manner, and I stand by it, but I need to explain this. Because I remember and you put this question to me and not Mr. Plazinic. You didn't ask me on what occasion when we met you meant, whether on the first occasion when we met or the second or the third in Stragari. It was a generally put question, and that's why my answer was as it was. And then now I've tried to explain that at some later point in time, I learned this from the media. And what is stated here, what I said to you in Belgrade, is still true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's an appropriate time for a break, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Curcin, before we broke we were talking about the Stragari facility, and let's stay focused on the Stragari facility. Did General Perisic ever visit Mladic at Stragari?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, once.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I can't remember precisely, but I believe it was in the early spring of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, during that visit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Excuse me, in the early autumn of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: During that visit, what position is General Perisic hold in the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: He was Chief of General Staff of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were you with General Perisic when he visited General Mladic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I wasn't with him. I happened to be there, and we met in the same facility at the same time on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you spend the day with General Mladic and General Perisic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: One could say so. It started mid-morning, and it lasted until afternoon, so you could say that we spent the majority of that day together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you describe what you did during that day?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: We weren't together all that time. We spent some time together. We talked, we walked through the woods, we played some chess. We also played cards, table tennis. We had lunch. And then we walked some more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, at the time the visit took place at Stragari was General Perisic aware that there had been indictments issued by this Tribunal for General Mladic and that there were warrants for his arrest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this question calls for speculation on behalf of the witness. Maybe the question should be reformulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't believe it calls for speculation. If the witness has a basis to answer, he can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you answer the question, please, General Curcin?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I can't, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But you were aware of it; correct?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Before the break we tried to clarify that I learned much later about the indictment, so I can't really say that in autumn of 1997 I was already aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you -- beside the visit that you and General Perisic and General Mladic had together at Stragari, did you hear that General Perisic visited General Mladic at Stragari on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: For the sake of the interpreters maybe I should clarify that this is not Strugari, but rather Stragari. I'm not sure if he ever visited him. I wasn't there so I couldn't claim that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you hear from others that he visited on occasions other than the time you were with him, General Perisic and General Mladic, at Stragari?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, as I -- let's talk about the facilities at both Stragari and Rajac. Is it standard operating procedure that someone who visits and stays at those facilities signs a register book, a guest register book, or records in any fashion his presence at those facilities?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. At Stragari, no. At Rajac, if you stayed there within a set package, and if you paid for your accommodation, food and so on, you would be registered in a ledger. Also you would be issued an invoice for the services and your car registration would also be recorded. At Stragari this was not the case because this was not the type of facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did General Mladic register either his person or his car or both at the facility at Rajac during his stays at that facility?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you suggest to persons who were at the Rajac facility not to keep records of General Mladic's visits at that facility?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you suggest to persons who were at the Rajac facility not to disseminate information to others about his visits at that facility?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: A large number of people recognised and loved General Mladic, but there were other people who did not respect him and who wanted to give him in, in exchange for some money for certain remuneration. So at the time it was important that it is not known where General Mladic was at a given moment of time. For these security reasons, for the sake of security of myself and other people who stayed there, other personnel, soldiers, officers, and also for the sake of security of Mladic himself, it was sensible to protect this information only to people who really saw him and who really knew about this. It was unnecessary to talk about this with anybody else. And this is why I told to some people not to talk about this in front of other people. This was my advice, fatherly advice, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So your advice was to avoid the possibility that General Mladic might be arrested on the warrants that were outstanding for him should it be known that he was at the facility at Rajac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm just looking for an answer given by the witness, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'm merely rephrasing a portion of the answer and seeking clarity on his answer that starts at line 16 and ends at line 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any response -- any reply, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is a wrong conclusion drawn by the Prosecution from something that is actually not included in the answer. And I believe that the Prosecutor cannot answer the question on the basis of such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you rephrase, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Curcin, the reason that you asked people not to disseminate information about General Mladic's whereabouts was because people might seek to arrest General Mladic and seek to claim the reward that was outstanding for him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Only up to a certain point. There were different individuals, renegades, from the security services, former members of our special units from Bosnia of NATO or SAS, and they might do this. We did not fear that members of our police, of our security units could do that. He at the time was not scared of these people, and it seems that he was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you discuss with your superiors and others about the presence of Mladic in the facilities at Rajac and Stragari?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, I did not discuss this either with my superiors or with people to whom I was superior. I did not discuss this with anybody, neither his presence nor my encounters with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: For the same reasons I mentioned before. Secondly, I was not ordered to do that. I did not give an order to do that, so there was simply no need for me to discuss this and to involve more people with information as to his whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General Curcin, you testified earlier that General Mladic had people with him, including a driver and a cook and security detail. During the war, did General Mladic drive himself, or did he have a driver during the war, personal driver?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Again you're talking about the war in Bosnia, or the war in 1999 in our country? I don't know because I was not in Bosnia for a long time. I was on duty there in 1967. I was not there thereafter, and I couldn't tell you whether he had a driver or whether he drove himself, or possibly he had another type of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On a number of occasions, General Curcin, General Mladic visited your family in Belgrade, didn't he? This is after the war ended in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: General Mladic visited me and my family on several occasions and I visited him and his family as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he have a driver when he visited you and your family in Belgrade, or did he drive himself?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't know. When he rang the doorbell, I live upstairs, I really don't know whether he had a driver downstairs in the parking-lot or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know the name of General Mladic's personal driver?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No, I do not know, and I also think that he changed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does the name Mladen Kenjic mean anything to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Does the name Gojko Crnjak mean anything to you? Do you know that person?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Jovan Djogo?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Jovan Djogo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him, this was a colonel who died several years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was his -- what were his responsibilities in respect of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't know, I knew him before in an earlier period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know an individual by the name of Darko Pecanac?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I do not know a Darko, I know a Pecanac, but I'm not sure whether his first name was Dragomir or something else. I know him, but I know for sure that his first name was not Darko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, when General Mladic was on the VJ properties at Rajac and later at Stragari and back again, how did he maintain himself in respect of provisions?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit 615 MFI on the monitor, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do that, you had a document on the screen here earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The record of the proceedings in Belgrade. What do you intend doing with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what was the 65 ter number of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's none, Your Honour. I have no 65 ter number for it. I brought it here not anticipating that I would need to use it as an exhibit, but given the nature of the answers, I put it on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic is on his feet. Let's hear what he has got to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this statement being included into evidence. I believe that what Mr. Harmon wanted to ask in relation to this statement is already in the transcript. It was read out, and it was included in the transcript. So I believe there is no need to include this into evidence as an entire statement pursuant to your direction number 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in your hands on this. I'm satisfied to have portions referred to admitted into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Registrar does know the pages that you referred to. Certainly page 1 was one of them. Those pages that were referred to and were shown on the monitor will be admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number. I don't know also without a 65 ter number how Madam Registrar is expected to link the exhibit number she's going to give to this statement, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have an identification number, it's 0614-56 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's use that. 061?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 4-5678. Fine. Under that reference, can we give it an exhibit number, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document with identification number 0614-5678 will be Exhibit P2216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There was, Your Honour, another item that was shown to the witness as well. It was a record of interview before the 2nd Municipal Court in Belgrade. I referred to this separate statement earlier when I was discussing with him under whose jurisdiction the facility at Rajac fell. And I referred him to a portion of that statement. That has been uploaded into the e-court, and it has a number. I'm told it has a reference of Curcin's statement, and the Registrar can identify that statement on the basis of that description. So I would ask that the portions referred to be given an exhibit number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I don't know -- yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same objection, Your Honours. I believe that in the transcript we already have the reference from these statements, from both these statements. We have it in the transcript, so I don't see the need to introduce not even a portion of the statement into the transcript. This is the way I understood your guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we have been doing this right through the trial. You put up a statement, you ask a few questions, and you tender the document. We have said that if you have -- if the statement is short and you have exhausted the entire content of the document, then there's no need to tender it because it is there, but if you've just referred to one or two parts of it, then we've always admitted. Isn't that the guide-line?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, my interpretation of your guide-line, paragraph 5, second sentence, I will read it out where you say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have this guide-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In these situations the quotation needs to be limited to the part of the transcript," I assume statement, "which is directly relevant for the question asked."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, let's read the entire paragraph. Okay. "The parties are instead encouraged to quote from the statement or transcript. However, the parties are requested to restrict such quoting to situations when it is strictly necessary for the understanding of the question asked. In such cases, the quote shall be restricted to the part of the transcript that is directly relevant to the question. Furthermore, in referring to your prior statement or testimony, the parties are asked to provide exact page and line references to the statement or transcript in question." The entire paragraph says nothing about what part of the document to admit, and what not to admit. What whole heading deals with cautioning parties from para-phrasing witness's statements, and thereby embellishing them. It has nothing to do with admission. But let me tell -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, the way I understand your guide-lines is not to admit too many documents, too many papers, and this is why in the transcript we already quoted a part of the statement, so I see no need to admit even this part of the statement because it is already in the transcript, and as such, it is part of the case file. This is the same thing we did when we read out parts of witness statements from other cases. So if an interested party reads out a sentence from a previous transcript and it is entered into the transcript, then there is no need to include the entire statement into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just give me the authority to that. Refer me it to a paragraph in the guide-lines that says so, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Harmon, do you see paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, and I'm satisfied to have just the portion of the statement that was referred to the witness entered into the record, as well as the first page of the statement which is identifying the record of the taking of the statement of the witness. And on that page as well it is an admonition or a description of an admonition that was given at the witness at the time that he gave this statement indicating that he was bound to testify and tell the truth, and he took an oath. So the portions of the statement for which I am seeking admission are just the first page of the document, which is a description of the record of the taking of a statement from the witness and a portion of the reference that deals with the facility at Rajac under his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem is that that paragraph forbids any admission of the statement at all under those circumstance -- under the circumstances of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Well, then I will withdraw, then, my request that this be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, General Curcin, I want to turn to another exhibit, or an exhibit. It is 615 MFI. General Curcin, if you could review that document on the screen before you. You will have to scroll up at some point. Scroll down. Have you finished reviewing the first part of this document, General Curcin?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I've seen it, but I have no intention of reading it. This is the first time I can see this. Could you please show me the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature on the last page of the document?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: No. I can see that this was not signed by the commander, but somebody on behalf of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Could you go to the first page of the document. General Curcin, this is a 1st Army headquarters administration document dated the 29th of August, 1997. It is an order. It relates to the issuing of moveables and fuel replenishment of VRS vehicles, and as you can see in the first paragraph, it is based on two decisions, orders. One 13-10-9 and another 13-10-12, both of which referred to the issuing of movables and fuel replenishment for vehicles in the VRS. Now, if we go down to paragraph 7, sir. Go down to paragraph 7 in the B/C/S, it's on the previous page at the bottom. Paragraph 7, General Curcin, discusses who can authorise the procurement and issuing of items in the order. It says: "Authorisation for the procurement and issuing of these items based on the request of the 1st Army headquarters administration organ will be by the 1st Army Chief of Staff, and, in his absence, by the 1st Army chief of operations affairs and training organ." Now, on the 29th of August, 1997, you were the 1st Army chief of operations affairs in the training organ, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DORDE CURCIN
utterances.text: I apologise, but this translation is not fully correct. And could I once again see the last page before I answer to your question. Yes, indeed, at the time I was chief of operations and training organ at the command of the 1st Army. My superior was the Chief of Staff of the 1st Army. At the same time, I was deputy of the Chief of Staff, and I stood for him in all the occasions when he was not present at his job, so I was at the given position. But this is the first time I'm seeing this order, and I have to say that neither me nor the Chief of Staff received this order.
